This form must be executed in duplicate when a child is transferred from a reservation to a nonreservation school. The Superintendent of the nonreservation school will retain the original for his files, and the duplicate shall be deposited in the reservation school records. The reservation superintendent should send to the Commissioner of Indian Affairs his certificate as provided by law. All the blanks must be properly filled in every case. If the information called for on any part of this blank is not known, that fact should be stated. No space should be left unfilled. Whether the parents are living or their names must be given. The person who signs the blank pertaining to the transfer should indicate his relation to the applicant by marking out the word "parent," "guardian," or "next of kin," leaving unmarked only the title appropriate to the signer. INDORSEMENTS. The laws relating to the transfer of Indian children from reservations and schools are as follows: That hereafter no Indian child shall be sent from any Indian reservation to a school beyond the State or Territory in which said reservation is situated without the voluntary consent of the father or mother of such child if either of them are living, and if neither of them are living without the voluntary consent of the next of kin of such child. Such consent shall be made before the agent of the reservation, and he shall send to the Commissioner of Indian Affairs his certificate that such consent has been voluntarily given before such child shall be removed from such reservation. And it shall be unlawful for any Indian agent or other employee of the Government to induce, or seek to induce, by withholding rations or by other improper means, the parents or next of kin of any Indian to consent to the removal of any Indian child beyond the limits of any reservation. (28 Stats., p. 906.) Provided, That hereafter no Indian child shall be taken from any school in any State or Territory to a school in any other State against its will or without the written consent of its parents. (29 Stats., p. 348.) That no Indian pupil under the age of fourteen years shall be transported at Government expense to any Indian school beyond the limits of the State or Territory in which the parents of such child reside or of the adjoining State or Territory. (35 Stat. L., 781.) The rules provide that— A pupil who has been regularly enrolled in a nonreservation school must not be taken to any other nonreservation school without the consent of both superintendents and the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, and superintendents will be held to strict accountability for such pupils taken to their schools. An Indian boy or girl 18 years old and over may, without the consent of parents or others, personally sign the application form on its being changed to suit the case; but in all cases where the parents are living they should first be consulted. Compliance must be given to all orders and instructions which have been promulgated in connection with the new course of study issued December 1, 1915. The information as to public school facilities called for in the certificate of the Superintendent (third page hereof) must be given, and all superintendents are especially directed to exhaust every means to secure enrollment of Indian children in the State public schools, pursuant to instructions heretofore issued in this regard. Nespelem Wash. Oct. 6, 1919 Dear friend, I am going to answer your letter which came on hand last two weeks ago. I am much glad to receive that school catalog which you have sent to me. I don't know when I'll go back to Cushman; it might be last of Oct. Nov. First of Aug. I went away from here. I ran over to Cusick & Spokane fair and I came back three weeks ago. That was after the children left for Cashman from here. I've been working ever since that. We're going to have Stampede fair here Oct. 8 to 10. I have got nothing else to say. So I'll say to close Yours Truly Friend David Brown Nespelem Wash Cushman Indian School Tacoma, Wash., May 28, 1919 Mr. Fred C. Morgan, Supt. Colville, Hespelem, Wash. Dear Sir: David Crow has requested me to write you for the transfer of $30.00 to his account at Cushman. This amount is to cover his expenses for the trip home, and leave a deposit here for his return to Cushman at the close of the summer vacation. If David has funds to his credit, I recommend the transfer of $30.00. Very respectfully, Superintendent. /MG 5-1142 DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR UNITED STATES INDIAN SERVICE Colville Agency, Nespelem, Wash., March 19, 1919. Supt. E. H. Hammond Cushman Indian School Tocoma, Washington. Dear Mr. Hammond: Here with is check #1274, in the sum of $25.00, which please deposit to the account of David Crow. David was just in my office and has advised me that he intends to return to your school tomorrow. Very respectfully, Fred C. O'Ryan Superintendent. SM/BW Incl. VACATION REQUEST FOR PUPIL. We, the undersigned, respectfully request that leave of absence be granted David Brown from June 15, 1918 to Sept. 5, 1918 to enable him to visit his home. We hereby agree to pay all expenses including round-trip railroad fares, sleeping-car fares, meals, lodging, stage fares, telegraph and telephone messages, and other incidental expenses connected with the visit. We further agree that said pupil shall be returned to the Chehalis school on or before the last day of the leave of absence. We further agree to deposit with the Superintendent of the school sufficient money to defray all expenses to be incurred, and should the pupils, or any one of them, fail to return to school at such time as may be agreed upon by the parents or guardian and the superintendent of the school in which the pupils are enrolled, the amount of money remaining with the superintendent, necessary to the return transportation of the pupil or pupils so neglecting to return, shall be forfeited to the Government; provided, however, that in all cases where it can be shown that there were justifiable reasons for the failure of the return of the pupil the forfeiture of the funds shall not take place. If the pupil neglecting to return is from a reservation, the superintendent of the reservation shall certify to the reasons for the nonreturn of the pupil or pupils. If a pupil's name is not on a reservation, then the certificate of some reputable, disinterested citizen of the community may be requested as to the reasons for the non return of the pupil or pupils. Morgan Nespelem, Washington Dear Sir: David Crow, a pupil from your reservation, wishes you to send him $20.00 for the purchase of some clothes. Respectfully, K-OHK Superintendent Colville Agency, Nespelem, Wash. November 7, 1917 Mr. David Crow, C/o Superintendent Hammond, Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Wash. Dear friend: I am in receipt of your letter of October 2 in which you ask for the sum of $25 from your bank account and in which you say that "I want you know very well that a boy going broke with his money becomes to be a thief in a little while." I am sorry to learn that you have cultivated such ideas. It is not at all necessary for a boy who has no money to spend to become a thief as you seem to think. Many white boys as well as Indian boys, who are not blessed with bank accounts as you are, manage to get along without stealing. You are supplied with every necessity at the school and because you do not happen to have money to spend for whatever you desire does not mean that you should become a criminal. There is no objection to your using some of your money for spending money and you will learn if you talk with the Superintendent that many of the boys at the school have asked for and have received some of their money for this purpose. The proper way for you to secure an allowance from your bank account is to make your request through your Superintendent who understands your needs better than I. I would, therefore, suggest that you talk with Superintendent Hammond and if he considers it advisable he will write me to that effect and an allowance from your bank account for spending money will be transferred to him for your benefit but I would suggest that the idea of stealing because you are without money in your pocket be given up by you at once. Very truly yours, Superintendent. David Crow is very anxious to have $25.00 sent to him. If he has the funds to his credit there, I recommend that the amount requested be sent him. I enclose a request from Carter Sloutier (Fisher) for more funds. At the present time, he is out of funds again. Very respectfully, Superintendent Tacoma, Wash. Feb. 20, 1918. Dear Friend: Well friend, I wish you please send me twenty five dollars of my account. I want buy a rain coat and get one side of tooth fixed and spent if you please. I am getting along fine here at Cushman School. How is everything over there. So I may close. Yours truly friend, Carter Sloutier Cushman Indian School, Tacoma, Washington, Jan. 28, 1918. Supt.
